idiom_name: Proc/lambda commands + SizedQueue + worker threads (Sidekiq in production)
implementation_notes: Ruby's blocks and lambdas make the Command hierarchy optional: a command is a `Proc`/lambda (typically `-> { service.place_order(id, qty) }`) that responds to `#call`, the repository is `Thread::Queue` or `SizedQueue` (whose `push` blocks when full, giving backpressure for free), and the executor is a pool of `Thread.new { loop { queue.pop.call } }` workers; because a lambda can also return its inverse, undo is an Array of procs. For anything durable, Sidekiq/ActiveJob is the production-grade realization of the same roles - job objects serialised to Redis, a worker pool as executor, retries and a dead set as the failure log - and the hand-built queue should not try to compete with it.
code_sketch:
queue = SizedQueue.new(256)                     # bounded == backpressure
history = []
workers = 4.times.map do
  Thread.new do
    while (cmd = queue.pop)
      history << cmd.call              # run the command, keep it for undo
    end
  end
end
queue.push -> { place_order(order_id, qty) }   # invocation, not execution
pitfalls: SizedQueue#pop blocks forever at shutdown: push sentinel values (or close via push(nil) per worker) or the process hangs instead of terminating.
An exception in a worker thread kills only that worker - and by default Ruby only warns (report_on_exception) - so the pool quietly shrinks; set abort_on_exception or rescue inside the loop.
The GVL means CPU-bound commands do not run in parallel: more worker threads do not buy throughput, so use a process-based pool (Sidekiq, fork) for CPU work.
Sidekiq's at-least-once delivery re-runs jobs after a crash; commands must therefore be idempotent or carry a deduplication key.
